Map: Strange Rocket Path
Author: rrrobyp

Object Use: 36 out of 50
The KRA portion of this map is your standard fare, for the most part at least. The thwump oneway push was cool, since some strategic timing and rocket placement was needed to cross through. Then there's the trapdoor triggering, which was a very unique little puzzle in itself.

Map Quality: 34 out of 50
The main problem here is that the first portion of the map (the non KRA part) required a lot of backtracking. It was the easy part, and then the rocket section came at the end. Since at one point you're unable to get another rocket if you mess up, you're forced to redo the lengthy first section. I've made this sound like a bad map, but other than those flaws it's actually quite creative and fun.

Total Score: 70


Map: Run, Thwump, Run!
Author: Korbachev

#5646 1 2005-12-13T04:11:04Z tktktk
I only get to do one of these this year for English, and this is actually almost twice as long as it needs to be. It comes from an idea I've been toying with for a while, and this gave me the motivation to finally write it, and I'm reasonably proud of how it came out. The name's kinda sappy, but it's supposed to portray innocence, in a way. The assignment was to write with a story with a few of the elements of of Stephen Crane's style in The Red Badge of Courage, so if you've read that you can tell me how I did in that department as well.

Please, comment and enjoy.


Angel Wings

Marten strode slowly but confidently to the cliffs edge. His dark and disheveled hair clung to his head from perspiration. He looked to the horizon. The sun shone brilliantly in the cloudless, liquid sapphire sky, and for a fleeting moment he imagined there to be another ocean mirroring the one that stretched endlessly out over a hundred feet below him. A warm breeze carried the aroma of fresh fish coming from one of the nearby cottages. Martens stomach growled at him resentfully at having been neglected for most of the day. Food can wait, he thought. This is much more important.

A boy and a girl from the village, each five or six years of age, were sparring playfully in the lush green grass not far away. Seeing Marten, they raced toward him cheerily and brimming with curiosity.

Whats that thing? It looks like a giant bird, the girl remarked.

She was pointing to a wooden contraption, long, slender, and sandy brown, that Marten clutched firmly with both hands. It did in some ways resemble a gull in flight, with wings of tightly stretched cloth. However, in place of the fowls body there was only a skeleton, the framework, with a sizeable hollow inhabited partially by various odd gears and mechanisms.

Yeah, shes a bird, agreed Marten proudly, And shell fly, too.

The pair stared at him for several moments with wide eyes that seemed to pierce the thin armor of his shallow confidence. In spite of the long months he had spent designing and constructing the bird in secret, doubts still throbbed painfully in the back of his mind. He pushed them away. She would fly, and so would he.

You think that thing will fly? retorted the boy. Youre just as crazy as your dad. Crazier, even.

Martens face immediately grew dark. His father was an inventor, but he was scorned by most of the village for not doing his share of the work. Only a few recognized that his creations were the only thing that kept them alive; the rest wrote him off as a daft and worthless tinkerer who consumed without producing. Thinking of this, Marten remembered his private vow to himself and to his father. He recalled the reason he had taken on this burden in the first place, and his resolve hardened.

Well, Ill be the one to show them just how crazy he is. Him and me both.

The sharp ache of adrenaline surged slowly through Martens muscles. He strapped himself into the bizarre aerial vessel, and took a few paces away from the precipice. Observing the sky again, he spotted a few speckled wispy clouds off in the distance. The sunlight streamed through them, painting them with whimsical pinks and oranges. He took this as a good omen, one of hope.

No turning back, Marten told himself. He took a few steps from the cliff, put on his most determined expression, and all at once sprinted at the void, attacking it before hesitations fingers could snare his mind in their cold grasp. As both feet left the ground, time appeared to slow, stop, rewind. It came to a halt at a long-suppressed memory of when Marten was but a toddler. His mother held him delicately in her arms. He giggled gleefully as she bobbed him up and down in midair. Without warning, her firm hold faltered, leaving him to hurtle to the merciless wooden floor below him. Just in time, her strong hands snatched him from harm, but as Marten snapped back to reality the memory was now playing out once again, and panic viciously engulfed him.

Marten plummeted sharply to the choppy swells below. Coming to his senses, he tugged wildly on two cords, jolting his craft to life. His trajectory flattened out, dangerously close to what seemed to be a vast expanse of death itself. A warm draft of wind caught the curved wings. To Martens astonishment, he began to ascend, though with painful sluggishness. Glints of silver waves caught his eye; they seemed infinitely more benevolent than they had been the moment before.

Looking to his right, he grinned as he saw the island, floating proudly and defiantly above water of ruffled silk. Martens isle was home to no more than a hundred people, and to their knowledge nothing existed apart from this odd mass of earth that gravitys stifling sheet of tyranny had overlooked. The lofty plateau was scattered with a variety of emerald vegetation and with small dwellings that nonchalantly spouted their gray smoke. At the edges, the cinnamon earth angled magnificently inward to form a jagged point at the base of the isle. Because there resided on the island no sufficient body of water, Marten naturally could not swim.

As he circled around, taking in his environment from this new perspective, it gradually dawned on him that there was little hope of ever rising high enough to return to dry land. Nightfall was making its approach, and he knew that the frigid air would be reluctant to support his already wavering craft. Looking helplessly to his island of refuge, he spotted two black vertical lines stretching into the sea, barely visible in the decaying light. Fishing ropes.

Marten worked vigorously at the controls, steering the bird sharply in the direction of his discovery. As he neared them he realized that he was hovering inches from the deep blue wasteland. It was impossible to reach his destination without plunging into it. He winced and braced for impact. As the icy doom devoured his body, eating its way from his feet up to his waist, he struggled for the line that swayed gently an arms length away. The waterlogged cloth, formerly his sole ally, now stubbornly held him back, and Marten was faced with a grim dilemma.

With no apparent alternative, Marten unfastened himself and paddled frenziedly towards the rope. After hauling himself from the water, he scrambled clumsily heavenward with no thought in his mind but of dry land. It took every kernel of strength in his body to propel himself to the towering summit. Having at long last arrived at his promised land, he sprawled onto the coarse grass, shuddering with cold and breathless exhaustion.

The two children who had shown such skeptical interest in Martens endeavors presently greeted him with enthusiastic shouts and mad frolicking.

Marten! We saw you! You were flying! they exclaimed together nearly unintelligible shrieks. They continued in their celebration for quite some time, but their excitement fizzled as they sensed Martens disheartened demeanor. He was looking away, weary and filled with a vague feeling of betrayal. He glanced dreamily up at familiar ivory stars with subdued acceptance.

Looks like the bird failed me after all.

Youre wrong, replied the girl. Her rounded face was saturated with an expression of complete conviction. She didnt fail you, and shes no bird either. Shes an angel. You rested your life in her hands, and she protected you. You were flying on angel wings.

#5773 1 2005-12-19T08:20:29Z tktktk
Over the next two weeks or so, I'll be giving a lecture on the intricacies of the enemies of N. I don't know how qualified I am to do so, but I got to thinking about just how much there is to each of these adorable little adversaries. Not only will this serve as a reference to others, but also as a way to organize my own thoughts on them. If this goes well, I may consider doing the same thing with the other, non-enemy objects. Oh, and if you have any comments or suggestions, I strongly encourage you to post them.

Each installment will be added to the first post. All right, here goes.



*****Segment 1: Introduction*****

There are nine types of enemies in N, the popular freeware game by Metanet Software. Each one possesses properties and abilities that the others do not. I will be discussing not only these abilities but also the proper techniques of taking advantage of them in effective level design. I have listed their proper, official names, but I will be using their common names for the remainder of the lecture.

Mines
Floorchasers (a.k.a. floorguards)
Homing turrets (a.k.a. rockets)
Gauss turrets (a.k.a. gausses)
Thwumps
Zap drones
Upgraded zap drones (a.k.a. seekers)
Laser drones (a.k.a. lasers)
Chaingun drones (a.k.a. chainguns)


The enemy types can be grouped in two fundamental ways, as follows:

1. Mines, floorguards, thwumps, zap drones, and seekers attack directly, while gausses, rockets, lasers, and chainguns fire projectiles.

2. Mines and zap drones are passive, meaning they do not purposely seek out the ninja. The rest are active (not necessarily mobile!), meaning that once the ninja is in their line of sight they will proceed to attack him.


The goal of enemies in N may seem exceedingly obvious, but there is more to it than first meets the eye. The goals of these ruthless homicidal machines, in the hands of a skilled mapmaker, are as follows:

1. To serve as obstacles that the ninja must overcome in order to achieve a certain goal. In conventional maps this will ALWAYS mean standing in the way of a switch, gold, or the exit. And of course, for this to be effective it requires the enemies to have a good balance of difficulty.

2. To give the illusion of being an obstacle. This can be used to take advantage of the player's sense of pride by projecting challenges that don't actually exist. This concept is illustrated by DDAs, in that there is no actual danger of death in spite of appearances to the contrary.

3. To be used for aesthetic purposes. Enemies can be placed to create artistic structure, balance, and color contrast within a map. Some mobile enemies are even walled in unreachable places on a level just to give a different feel than it'd otherwise present without.


Now that you understand the basic ideas and purposes for the enemies as a whole, we can have a look at each one individually.



*****Segment 2: Mines*****

Mines are by far the most versatile enemies in N. Put in the simplest of terms, they are tiny sections of space that the ninja cannot traverse. In spite of their apparent relative harmlessness, a single mine can render an easy level incredibly difficult (yet possible) to beat. They can be used for a vast number of purposes, and they will be laid out in detail in the following section.

One of the most fundamental properties of the mine is that it cannot move. How, then, can mines be so utterly difficult to avoid? The answer lies in the movement of the ninja himself. When the ninja moves towards a mine, the effect is more or less the same as if the mine were moving toward the ninja. When placing mines, we can take advantage of two basic elements. Note that these elements also apply to all other enemies; it's just that they are most visible in the case of mines.


1. Player movement: By placing mines closer to other enemies or solid barriers such as tiles we are giving the player a smaller margin of error and therefore a higher chance of death. As the player moves toward a mine, he is forced to make additional movements in order to avoid it. Also important to consider are items that dramatically alter the player's movement, such as launchpads and bounce blocks.

2. Gravity: This form of movement is often taken for granted since it is not controlled by the player. The downward direction of gravity pulls the ninja back down to earth, as well as into any mines below him. Couple that with momentum and a level with merely multiple, floor-ridden mines where the player spawns at the top could prove quite challenging.


Mines often serve as impassable barriers that the ninja cannot get through. These barriers can be used in conjunction with tiles or without them. The benefit of a lack of tiles is that all other enemies can pass through mines, while the ninja cannot. Conversely, using tiles with mines means that enemies cannot pass through either, and also may allow the ninja to traverse only specific areas of the tiles.

Mines are excellent for use as stationary guards of gold and switches when in close proximity to them; this is just a small touch that adds completeness to a map. Also, when used in conjunction with other enemies, mines are capable of forcing the ninja to negotiate difficult situations. Their presence means that there are less routes for the ninja to escape from other nearby enemies.

Using many mines together in an effective minefield can be one of the most challenging aspects of level design. It is extremely important to maintain a balanced difficulty throughout. Ideally, the mapmaker plans out multiple routes, each requiring differing jump heights, making use of the elements listed above. However, it should give the player the impression that he is finding an uncharted path through the mines on-the-go. Because the ninja's gravity is out of the player's control, going through a minefield in freefall is the closest thing one can get to having active, moving mines. Constructing a freefall minefield uses essentially the same strategies as a that of a normal one, given the obvious exception that momentum and gravity must be taken into account for.

Finally, there is the aesthetic element. Mines, quite obviously, are red. Together with the yellow of gold and the blue of some other enemies (primarily zap drones), a map can include each of the three primary colors, which can make a map much more pleasing to the eye. In addition, mines can be added to space not devoted to gameplay, sometimes along with tiles or other objects, to make a map appear less empty.


*****Segment 3: Floorguards*****

Floorguards run back and forth across any flat surface when the ninja comes into its line of sight. The line of sight extends to all the empty tiles to either side of the floorguard, and stops when it hits a tile. They have a few basic functions, which can be used in many variations.

One of the most important things to acknowledge about floorguards is that they are the only enemy that is faster than the ninja is. This point is vital in understanding the mechanics of gameplay involving them. When the ninja is running on a long flat surface with a floorguard following close behind, the floorguard will eventually catch up, forcing the ninja to jump and allow it to pass (and then, if the ninja must land on the same strip of land, rebound back for the other direction once more).

This aspect is especially useful in corridors. Dead-end corridors have only one opening, while through corridors have more than one. In some corridors, floorguards can serve as barriers that completely block an opening. In dead-end corridors this effect would be permanent, and is one of the most common causes of "undeath" (possibly also "pseudodeath," meaning that the level becomes impossible to complete). In through corridors, the player simply has to find another, unblocked opening.

A corridor that is only one tile high gives the ninja no room to evade a floorguard, which means he will either exit the corridor or perish. In both types of corridors, the ninja can be forced to scramble in and out before a floorguard can get to him. Corridors that are 1.5 or 2 tiles high, however, give the ninja just enough space to let the floorguard pass, creating a lot of high-tension moments. This is especially true when other enemies, particularly mines, are placed in the corridors.

The floorguard does not always have to serve as a "chaser"; it can also be used as an extra little nuisance when the ninja isn't moving much horizontally. When the ninja is jumping to get gold or switches slightly above him, the floorguard forces the player to make further small jumps that are outside of his original plan.

Floorguards are effective as active guards when gold and switches are placed on or above a small plot of ground. This forces the ninja to spend only a split-second touching the ground, lest he be smashed into oblivion by an electronic, bloodlusting little puppy. When on a one-tile long horizontal surface, floorguards can be used as slightly larger, intelligent mines. This comes in handy when one wants to add a tiny bit more challenge than a regular mine would offer.

Something to keep in mind when placing multiple floorguards: if they are placed away from the ends of their line of sight, the ninja can often attract all of them off to one side. Because they are on top of each other, they [v]overlap and more or less merge into one floorguard[/b] from that point on.

Now comes the aesthetic point. Floorguards have bluish-green eyes and border, which gives one element of color to a map that can be used along with gold and mines. They also make excellent centerpieces when surrounded by the aforementioned objects, albeit being slightly asymmetrical in design.


*****Segment 4: Rockets*****

Rockets are one of the most versatile and interesting enemies in the game. They can also be one of the most enjoyable when used correctly. Rockets launch from a stationary turret. They are fired when the ninja comes into the turret's line of sight. A line of sight is created anywhere where the ninja is not blocked by tiles or doors. The rocket will then travel in the ninja's direction until it hits a tile, a door, or the ninja himself.

The player will use tiles and doors to his advantage to destroy rockets. This generally involves either outrunning the rocket or getting out of the way quickly when the rocket is close to both the ninja and a door or tile. In enclosed spaces, the problem is not with how to destroy the rocket but how to keep from being destroyed oneself. The mapmaker must keep this in mind and create some means of escape. In other words, tiles and other objects are as much of an obstacle as the rocket itself.

When rockets are used in open spaces with objects such as one-ways and bounce blocks, they will seldom be destroyed. They will persistently attack the ninja, forcing the player to make use of more advanced evasion methods. The rockets will tend to circle around the ninja. When used in conjunction with bounce blocks, rockets often offer a very enjoyable challenge, as the player can use its added movement abilities such as dips and increased jumps while the rocket is just as much unimpeded by the blocks themselves. Good object placement in open-rocket areas can be one of the most exhilarating situations in a level.

While using rockets, it is essential to remember that the launcher will not fire another rocket until the first is destroyed. This principle is crucial to maps that force the player to keep a rocket from being destroyed. Placing the turret in a corridor housing the exit ensures that the it will fire on the ninja unless the rocket is kept alive. This concept can be used to make the rocket trail the ninja through the entire level, or only a small part of it by drawing the rocket out of a corridor. When playing a map, the player must be careful not to be too close to a turret when its rocket is destroyed although it has a minor reload time before blasting another one off.

In addition, one highly advanced trick a player can use is to confuse a rocket by initiating a close call and getting directly behind it, thereby drawing it away from the ninja for a short time. It can also be used to draw them away from or into a wall, as the situation demands.

When dealing with multiple rockets, keep in mind that over time they will converge and essentially become one. This makes things significantly easier, so the mapmaker should take this into account. Placing turrets close to one another aggravates this problem. If tiles are arranged so that rockets are easily destroyed, rocket convergence shouldn't be a very large factor. When multiple rockets are on drastically different paths, the difficulty of movement multiplies as well, unless some or all of the homing projectiles can be destroyed or outrun.

Rocket turrets are a very dark red, not a very good source of aesthetics as far as color is concerned. However, they can balance a map very well, even when the bulk of the map is on one side.


*****Segment 5: Gausses*****

Gausses, like rockets, consist of a stationary turret and a projectile. Unlike rockets, however, the moving part of the gauss is a crosshair which appears when the ninja is in the turret's line of sight (that is, when its view is not obscured by tiles or doors). The crosshair follows the ninja, and when it gets close enough fires an instantaneous shot in a straight line. If any part of the ninja intersects the line (however thin it is), the result is instant death.

Although they can be overlooked very easily, gausses actually have seven phases of tracking upon firing. They are as follows:

1. No crosshair
2. Small crosshair
3. Medium crosshair
4. Large crosshair
5. Red box & crosshair
6. Instantaneous shot (red box & crosshair)
7. Gray box & crosshair
8. Reverts to 2, unless the ninja evades the turret's line-of-sight by then

In rare cases, they may skip a step. The size of the crosshair, and therefore the gauss's tendency to fire, is related to the ninja's distance both from the crosshairs and from the line of fire. In avoiding gauss fire it is especially important to be observant for the aiming reticule's red box, because the turret will fire approximately a quarter of a second after it appears. The crosshair will also stop moving the moment the red box appears, allowing a slight chance for a reprieve.

An interesting behavior is introduced when multiple gausses are tracking the ninja - their crosshairs get closer and closer together until they eventually converge. When they converge completely they will fire exactly in unison. This formation is broken when only one gauss shoots (when they are not perfectly aligned) or when the ninja is out of one of the turrets' line of sight. It is also extremely important to keep track of which crosshairs belong to which turrets when working with multiple gausses, as it is not always readily apparent since their targeting reticules show no link to their original turrets until they fire or upon initial appearance.

Gausses placed in open spaces are usually quite easy to avoid and outsmart, particularly when the ninja isn't moving back and forth across the line of fire. Keep in mind that the farther away the crosshairs are from the ninja, the faster they move, which means that most of the time it's virtually impossible to outrun a gauss completely for any lengthy period. The speed of a turret's aiming reticule acts something like a radioactive half-life (chemistry), in that they slow down the closer they come to the final point. If the ninja is, in fact, required to zigzag multiple times across the line of fire, objects and tiles should be placed to allow free movement in the immediate area.

Always remember that gausses can fire from a great distance across the playing field. This often occurs when one least expects it (because the line of sight appears to be blocked at times), and results in many frustrating deaths. When designing maps it is good to keep this idea in mind.

In tighter spaces maneuvering past gausses can be considerably more difficult, especially when coupled with mines and other enemies. Because the ninja is closer to the crosshair and line of fire, gausses tend to fire more often than in other situations. They are good for creating tense moments, but be careful to give the player at least a little breathing room. In general, avoid "dead-ends," where the gauss gets a cheap and easy shot at a cornered ninja. When used in corridors that are one tile wide, gausses present a different sort of challenge. The player must often lure the gauss into firing in one direction while getting through the turret to the other side before it fires again. This can often require a good amount of quick thinking and strategy.

Gausses are somewhat reddish in color, but have very little bearing on the overall color balance of a map. They act as excellent balances and centerpieces, however, and can bring a sense of completeness to a map.


Next segment: Thwumps

#125843 2 2005-12-22T06:55:48Z tktktk
Here you go. I hope you don't mind that I picked on your spelling errors. The biggest overall problem I had with your maps was that you had a lot of very frustrating uses of chainguns in open spaces. Also, you've submitted 3-4 to Numa already. I was assuming all the Legacy levels were supposed to be new.

I had a blast with these, you did a great job on 'em.


0-0: Way to start things off. I like the race-type element, its simple but it helps the map flow really well.

0-1: Ahh. Gotta love that complex drone path goodness. Well, not really complex individually, but overall anyway.

0-2: That lowest piece of gold is quite a nice challenge. Things are well laid out, so it never becomes frustrating.

0-3: I know spelling isnt your strong point, but I might as well critique that as well. Homicide, not Hommocide. The drone timer concept works well, but its used pretty simplistically. My main concern is the cheapness factor of the chainguns.

0-4: Ive tried making these Lofty-style thwump levels before, but they never come out right. This works great though.

1-0: Oh, is it ever worth it. Very unique jumps displayed here. Thats becoming more and more rare these days.

1-1: Great, great minefield map. The launchpads kept it from becoming too mundane.

1-2: Surprisingly easy considering its one of your traditionally difficult hallway maps. Use of thwumps is just different enough to be interesting.

1-3: Freakin cool use of thwumps; Ive seen the uses before but never presented so well. Plus its got just a tad of survival map element to it, and that sets it apart.

1-4: Wow. Now thats a drone map. I had a lot of fun figuring out the route for this.

2-0: It got a little repetitive, but aside from that this was fairly decent.

2-1: Its so easy, yet I seldom find maps as fun as this one. Well done.

2-2: Ah, Flash. Where would we be without it? The object placement was excellent and fit the tileset well, particularly the slide-type thing.

2-3: Cute as a button. The minelessness (not mindlessness) as well as the enemy variety and launchpads make this a quirky take on a traditional map style.

2-4: I like the name. I like the launchpad. I like the drones. I like the map.

3-0: This one I kind of disliked. It worked fine if you were just aiming for completion, but the chainguns became a lot more frustrating if you tried to go for the gold.

3-1: This had several good and bad points. The chainguns tended to kill me at the very beginning unless I really concentrated my first jump, which I didnt really like. The rocket could be a bit of a nuisance, sometimes launching at the worst possible moment. The launchpads had a nice flow, but getting up to them required a walljump thus rendering them somewhat useless anyway. That said, I enjoyed the map in spite of its flaws.

3-2: Usually Im not one to like maps scattered with this many turrets, but I actually had a lot of fun with this. Finding the perfect route required a bit of strategy and was highly rewarding.

3-3: Very satisfying action puzzler. Sort of reminded me of one of blue_tetris maps.

3-4: Are you supposed to include this in Legacy since youve already submitted it to Numa? Anyway, not bad, reminiscent of some of Metanets levels, like 2-0 and 39-3.

4-0: Pretty cool, reminds me of stepselfs thwump action-puzzles. There are definitely a lot of ways you can use them to your advantage.

4-1: Whew, those floorguards are tougher than they have any right to be. The spot-on item and enemy placement make this one of my favorites so far.

4-2: This requires a lot of 45-degree angle drone avoidance; its difficult with it and even more so without it. Thankfully the map isnt long enough to get overly frustrating.

4-3: This just reeked of quality. Almost all of my movements seemed planned beforehand even though they were my own. One exception lay in the two upper bounce blocks. I would move them both down half a snap; that should make things run a little more smoothly in that section.

4-4: There were some issues with the chainguns here (as they usually dont mix well with open spaces), but they worked better than I expected them to.

5-0: Again, excellent placement. The launchpad route was very easy, but Im glad it wasnt made too obvious.

5-1: Nothing spectacular here. The chaingun room is nice for a separate challenge.

5-2: I thought the floorguard switches were pretty tough, and having to go through two of them made it just a tad too much so. The laser section was great, very well-balanced.

5-3: Really quirky and surprisingly difficult grab bag type map. Getting back up the right side, in particular, was way tougher than it looked.

5-4: The system of gausses works nicely. Not a whole lot else to say.

6-0: Pretty intense if youre trying for the gold, particularly the upper stash. Otherwise, its business as usual.

6-1: Repressed? Oh noes! Never seen quite this type of oneway usage, and the chaingun performs pretty decently despite the open space.

6-2: I liked the differences in towers. They were subtle enough that I didnt notice at first, but they were there. Each had its good points as far as flow.

6-3: I love the way the drones are timed to converge right when you get there but still leave enough room for you to slip through. That section in general is just really cool.

6-4: Fantastic. Great concept with the use of thwumps. The gausses can get really annoying though.

7-0: I really and thoroughly enjoyed this. It feels like this is precisely the way the floorguards were meant to be used. Great use of partial cover with the chainguns.

7-1: The rotational symmetry is put to good use here. Just a fun map to play overall.

7-2: Getting pinned down by lasers in the little exit room aint exactly fun. The rest of the map is just dandy though.

7-3: What in the everloving awesome? My favorite map thus far. The tileset, the thwumps, the lasers, everything collaborates to make this what it is. Well done.

7-4: Mmm. Intensely evil yet rewarding claustrophobic goodness. Yummy.

8-0: The way the mines are scattered strikes me as aesthetically ugly, if that makes any sense. The way some of them are in lines just rubs me the wrong way. Plays great though.

8-1: Straightforward, simple and elegant. Thats really the best way to describe it. Harder than it looks, too.

8-2: Its easy to get sniped from afar, but every time I do I get the feeling that I should have been paying more attention. The object placement is especially good here.

8-3: Words cant really describe how cool that first torrent of thwumps is. Its a bit of a shame the six bottom down-facing thwumps werent put to good use.

8-4: This shouldnt have been that hard, but it had me going a little nuts until I finally beat it. Creative use of thwump riding and trapdoors; too bad that rocket is too insanely persistent for me to give a care.

9-0: Nothing special really. Waiting for the drones to come out of that corridor was supremely yawn-inducing, although I suppose I was meant to use that time for getting gold.

9-1: Well this is so Metanet its silly. High drone count equals high intensity.

9-2: Whoa. Fast-paced, bewildering, and I loved every second of it. I always maintain just enough control to keep myself alive, and thats what keeps up the thrill of the level.

9-3: Eeew. You have several maps like this, and I dont very much like any of them. Its mainly the chainguns. I dont detest them in themselves, but there are some situations where they work and some where they dont.

9-4: Once again, the chainguns were ridiculously annoying. Very unfun. The rest of the map wasnt bad though.

10-0: A thing of beauty. The top and the bottom play very differently. Nice name, too.

10-1: Er whats with the tiles on the right wall? Things work out better with the upper left bounce block than with the upper right one, so I would think youd want to change that.

10-2: A masterpiece. Im serious. It performs its function perfectly, and the concept is just beautiful.

10-3: Very good map for how pure and simple it is. Those rockets discourage you from just plunging into things.

10-4: Stunning use of rotational symmetry. Ive hardly ever seen it used to further the gameplay as much as it has been here.

11-0: I thought this was designed really well. The two switches by the exit changed things up a little; Ive never seen something like that before.

11-1: I have a level in my pack that uses the same concept as this one, but this totally puts mine to shame. Great work.

11-2: What can I say, except well done again. The two unguarded switches and the gold near them stood out to me as just a little bit out of the ordinary (in a good way).

11-3: Very confusing with the different pathways and switches, but definitely nice for a change. I enjoyed it.

11-4: Awesomely quirky level. Almost LV-esque, in an odd way. I didnt like that starting wall jumping segment at first, but it grew on me as I discovered it to be a kind of minigame in itself.

12-0: I like the tileset quite a bit. Good use of a simple theme throughout the map.

12-1: Not all that suspenseful, actually. Pretty basic step lightly theme, and its appropriately somewhat difficult to get the necessary height.

12-2: That middle section is just golden. Very fun map to play, and I like how the seeker drones factor into it.

12-3: Nice tileset, it goes really well with the lasers. The use of doors is very interesting as well.

12-4: Dying, not dieing. The number of rockets gave it a high difficulty, but the object placement ensured that things never became too frustrating. This is high-quality work.

13-0: Is that supposed to be one word or two? Either way, excellent job on this. I particularly liked the use of chainguns.

13-1: Rockin tileset. Obviously this isnt meant to be a full-blown map, but what is there is pretty great. I was slightly annoyed that you couldnt drop down on the exit switch from above since the rocket would usually get you.

13-2: Its pretty easy to complete with almost zero interference from chainguns. Even so, I enjoyed experimenting with different ways of beating it.

13-3: As simple as it was, it was also genuinely fun. Reminds me of a smaller version of one Metanet level. Getting the exit switch required some careful planning.

13-4: Cant say I cared much for this one. There really wasnt anything wrong with it, but it definitely isnt one of your better maps.

14-0: This sort of appealed to the highscorer in me. There was a lot of strategic movement because of the rockets, and the grid placement of the gold for some reason encouraged me to get it in the shortest possible time.

14-1: The lasers stood out as the best part of this map. The rest was nice, but I could have done without it.

14-2: There was one really simple completion route that I could find; the other ways were more of a challenge, particularly if you wanted the gold.

14-3: I didnt expect to enjoy this as much as I did. The bounce blocks were ideal for double jumps, and the bottom section was as fun as it was chaotic.

14-4: Very interesting tileset. There are lots of different ways to get the gold, but with some of the pieces I felt like there was supposed to be some specific way of getting them, and I just couldnt find it.

15-0: The switches and the gold were both fun to get in their own way. I liked the placement of the mines next to the switches.

15-1: There was too much going on in this map for my tastes, mainly in the center strip. It played nicely, though, and the unlockable gold was interesting.

15-2: Both intense and a nice, refreshing change. I liked the laser/thwump combo, the drone not so much. Great work overall.

15-3: Dalai, not Dali. I like the part where you walljump to get over the row of mines. Im not sure if this is intentional or not, but you can get the switches without passing all the way through the oneways.

15-4: I love this, its so simple and well realized. I cant believe it hasnt been done before.

16-0: Very interesting. Its basically a KRA map, but its less constricting than most. It was cool that the rocket needed to be going clockwise or counterclockwise depending on the segment.

16-1: This was really intense, but really great. The laser and the chaingun were very difficult to get past, but it was possible with the right timing.

16-2: Easy, and great fun to play. Good use of point jumping, among other things.

16-3: This wasnt quite as interesting and different as it looked. The top was better than the bottom, in my opinion.

16-4: I liked the use of the one-way gold structures. You were forced to get in and out quickly because of the rocket.

17-0: Whoa. Much harder than it looks (the zap drones in particular), and very very well designed. A blast to play, great job.

17-1: Theres a feel of randomness to the firing of the lasers that I really dislike. The switches shielded by oneways are an interesting challenge to get.

17-2: One of the best so far. The lasers are ridiculously well placed, and theres always a way out of being pulverized by them, so if you die you have only yourself to blame.

17-3: I really like the idea of getting the gold in that side room while youre waiting for the thwump to come down. The mines by the exit, on the other hand, are just irritating.

17-4: This is a very weird map. Personally I dont think its up to your standards. Im not sure if its anything in particular, but it doesnt come off as being of very high quality.

18-0: The lower laser always tends to get me at the very end. Its kind of annoying. Other than that I enjoyed it very much.

18-1: Those three little rockets made things incredibly hectic. Sometimes it was exciting, but other times they bugged the heck outta me.

18-2: The lasers were very tough to get past, especially if you wanted the gold.

18-3: One little thing here that kept things a little different is how you couldnt get into the left room simply, even though it seemed like you could. You could wall jump or corner jump, and I thought it was neat that the latter option was kept open.

18-4: I liked how you could make a timed fall and have the thwump carry you back up or go in and out quickly before the thwump could smash you.

19-0: The switches were rather boring, but the left, right, and bottom gold offered some creativity.

19-1: I agree, they should stay where they belong. The concept was good, but in practice in meant a lot of waiting around, which obviously isnt good.

19-2: Its been done before, by you even, and better at that. Kind of weird that the left drone doesnt have any gold.

19-3: Really nice. It does exactly what it sets out to do, and it does it well. I kind of wish that there was a little bit of reward for taking a ground route, though.

19-4: I couldnt have picked a better level to end on. The tileset reeks of organic elegance, and the gold/mine things works great along with it.

#126172 10 2005-12-23T07:02:40Z tktktk
Okay, I've edited most of the maps you had problems with. They should be somewhat easier now, so try 'em out.

Here are my revisions:

002: Moved the two bottom tiles one tile to the right. Getting back up from the bottom will be a little easier, though I never thought it hard at all in the first place.

003: Moved almost everything up one tile except the bounce block, made minor tweaks to tileset and drone positions.

004: Replaced the two gausses with one centered one, changed the drone positions, added normal doors. It's noticeably more fun now, I think.

005: I switched around which switches open which doors. This should make getting the exit switch slightly easier because you have a flat surface to run on if you leave one of the doors locked.

006: Traded two rockets and one gauss for two gausses and one rocket.

010: Took out a floorguard, changed ninja and remaining floorguard positions. Significantly easier now.

011: Moved the exit switch half a snap to the left.

013: This was a hard decision for me. I wanted to keep this a tough map, so I just took out the gauss turret. It makes it more forgiving near the end, but it also gives the map an emptier feel. Not a whole lot I can do, though.

015: Moved the exit switch up a quarter snap. You dont have to be quite as careful with that jump now.

016: Moved the exit a little to the left, and the oneway/mine dealies a quarter snap to the right.

028: Shoved some of the gold and mines left, giving more room to walljump.

032: This one I redid almost completely, except for the tileset. It seems a lot less deliberate and contrived now, I think. Might be kind of tough, though.

035: In case you hadn't noticed, I changed the name. If maximo can in fact keep his 3-4, I don't want things to be confusing.

042: I gave a little more running room for two of the bounce blocks. In other news, this is now actually possible to beat.

049: You guys are no fun. Sigh I scaled down the difficulty somewhat, took out that mine, etcetera. Then I had to go and change the name from insanely hard to just hard".

#127416 12 2005-12-27T22:47:23Z tktktk
Nice edits overall. Here you go:

2-3: Didn't notice much difference in the laser. Still a great map.

3-1: I actually don't think this is any better. The chainguns are easier to avoid in the beginning, but harder at the end.

3-4: Fantastic. I love the x-axis symmetry. It's such pure and simple fun.

4-3: The top works great now. Nice job.

5-2: A little less engaging, but way less tedious and frustrating. Less is more.

9-1: I don't see the point of it, but again, it's certainly not any worse.

10-2: Looks much better now.

10-4: More gold is always good. Still great.

11-4: Aww... I kinda liked those floorguards. But you're right, they would make it pretty frustrating to die right there.

13-0: Never had a problem with that jump, but again, no worse. Besides, it looks good with the open exit.

13-4: Eh. Still don't care for the map.

16-3: Interesting changes. I think I do like this better.

#130443 3 2006-01-07T09:36:51Z tktktk
Grr... I commented on all of these and then it was all deleted when my post didn't get through. Here we go. Fantastic stuff overall.

2-0: Excellent small map. Seems like it should be generic, but there's just something special about it. The launchpads are a nice quirky touch and add to the flow.

2-1: Obviously a remake of Artificial Intelligence, and it works surprisingly well in the limited space. The thwumps were very unthreatening though.

3-0: Odd name, I thought. It's a very simple jump puzzler, and there was just enough substance for me to enjoy it.

3-2: This is what I'd call a "Metanet cookie cutter map". Usually that would be a bad thing, but this happens to play very well.

4-0: This should be taken out since it's been submitted to Numa. Great mine/bounceblock field, but I was kind of weirded out by the stuff on the bottom.

4-2: The inside was interesting (I'm glad you made it asymmetrical), but I got a kick out of just timing the run up one side under the drone.

4-3: This one was just all right. The rocket/floorguard combo was nice, but I feel like I've played this type of thing before.

6-0: Great chaingun bunker map. There are plenty of safe places where you can duck down at any time. The open spaces are harder to traverse, but never overly so.

6-1: I didn't care all that much for the structure and pattern of it, but it was still pretty good. The chainguns did their job well.

7-4: Reminds me of a more minimalistic maximo map (woo alliteration). The drones applied plenty of pressure, but I always had a chance to slip away in time.

8-0: The way this is set up is brilliant. I love unlocking all the gold and then cruising right on through the bottom at the end.

8-1: The way you sorted the drones to move in two separate rows on the bottom was brilliant. Pretty decent overall.

9-0: Good tough map. Getting back up forced me to make some very difficult maneuvering. Kind of reminds me of my map Ka.

9-3: It was interesting working with the seeker drones on the way back from getting the exit switch. I don't like the way the minefield looks, but it plays well.

10-0: Ah. Two routes, one easy/boring, one harder/rewarding. I like it, and it works well as a column starter.

11-1: This was the only one I actually disliked. I think it would be a little better if you put some gold in between the mines or something.

12-0: Very open and fun. My favorite part of this map was getting to the top section using the side thwumps rather than the middle one.

14-0: I love the way that first drone is timed to be by the exit switch right about when you get there. It makes for some cool situations.

15-2: By far my favorite of this bunch. The concept of keeping the drones out of the way so you don't slam into them making that big jump is fantastic. The difficulty is tough but well-balanced. Great job.

15-4: You get some real style points for this one. The platforms were laid out nicely, and the bottom provided a cool alternate route. The top rooms were classic LV style.

Due to the number of maps that have gotten abnormally high ratings as of late, I've decided to start this thread. Here are the rules:

1. Don't rate a map down just because it's in this thread. Rate each map only how you think it should be rated.

2. Post only maps that you deem to be grossly overrated, to the point where either it looks as though there has been foul play involved, or a large number of clueless members have rated it in a way that runs totally counter to common sense.

3. As a rule of thumb, posters should only post maps that they believe should be rated at least 1.5 ninjas lower than they are.

4. This works the same way as the Map-Rating Thread; you must rate a map for every map you post and state which map you have rated in your post. That way we can ensure that all these maps get the ratings they deserve.

5. Unlike the Underrated Map Thread, however, you may post your own maps.

I'll get us started with Speedy N Deadly.

#137106 2 2006-01-29T17:10:34Z tktktk
Overall these were good, but not quite as good as I'd expect from you. I think a lot of it is a personal dislike of the style in some of the maps rather than actual low quality. I feel like I'm being too harsh, but there were only a couple of these that I would consider truly great.

In case you didn't see, we're planning on you and LV both having 50 maps rather than 100. That should give you a little extra time for tweaking and whatnot.

0-0: Very difficult for an opening level, I think. Concept is great, though, and I like the tile squeeze.

0-1: Decent fun. Good use of mines. Top gold is very tough to get.

0-2: Cool usage of perpendicular jumping. It might make more sense to put the gold towards the middle since that would give more reward for the tougher route.

0-3: Interesting. I like the way the seeker drone fits in with the others. The start point gives a good way to launch into things.

0-4: I like the way the platforms are set up. However, it might be better to lose the regular switch and just have the exit switch replace it.

1-0: The way you managed to downsize the amount of space while maintaining "bunker" gameplay is amazing. There are some cheap deaths, but they're kind of unavoidable. Great work.

1-1: Dang it. I had a level a lot like this (not for Legacy), but this one's way better. The way you're launched gives a nice sense of exhiliration.

1-2: A very different take off of my map "The Beauty Of It". I don't know what our stance is on glitches like this, but this may not be allowed in. Extremely cool idea though.

1-3: I loved the bottommost gold with the gauss. The rest was pretty good as well.

1-4: Plays well enough I guess. The style of gold placement varies a little weirdly.

2-0: Hmm. Climbing around was kinda fun. Could do with a tad more gold. (I'm quite the gold Nazi, aren't I?)

2-1: Good map. It'd be nice if you could use the center thwump to get to the launchpad without being massacred. The other approach works perfectly well, it's just good to have more than one option.

2-2: I like the use of gausses. The whole trapdoor/oneway system is a little weird though.

2-3: The rotational symmetry is a little inconsistent on some of the tiles above the left switch and below the right switch. Pretty well balanced.

2-4: The little rooms on the top and bottom were a little different, as was the overall design.

3-0: Great small map. The drones give you just enough space to move around.

3-1: I really liked this one. It's difficult to just cruise through it, but there are a lot of approaches that you can use to avoid the chaingun fire effectively.

3-2: Pretty good hard puzzler. Keep in mind that getting the gold should be worth it; you might wanna add a little more.

3-3: Very nice high-flying level. Both the KRA element and the teleporters work well.

3-4: Plays just differently enough to justify itself. Again, there's the tile issue.

4-0: Eep. Those little crevasses don't give you much room to hide. Good thing you can usually retreat to the center section.

4-1: The thwump system makes you plan things out just a bit. The mine by the exit switch can be rather irritating though.

4-2: This has got a really good flow to it. The launchpads are set up well, as are the enemies.

4-3: It's not much, but what there is looks excellent.

4-4: I liked the top better than the bottom, although both were good. Lots of different routes for getting the top done, and that's always a good thing.

5-0: The design is sparse, but still manages to be both stylish and functional. The lasers work great.

5-1: One of the best so far. Very polished, and the way the beginning works with the drones is creative.

5-2: The use of launchpads is stupidly fun, and the rest is above average as well.

5-3: The beginning with the first switch has an excellent flow if it's done correctly. There's some good variety in the different parts of the map.

5-4: A stepselfian thwump puzzle. I'd suggest getting rid of the mines touching the thwumps, just to ease the difficulty and give the map a cleaner look. However, that could take away from the puzzle element.

6-0: In case you didn't realize it, this one has no exit. The drones and the oneway/locked door combos are intriguing.

6-1: I can see that some thought went into this design. Using the thwump squeeze to propel yourself into the exit was a great ender.

6-2: Call me impatient, but I dislike the two thwumps at the beginning. The upper gold was a challenge.

6-3: Mind-blowingly cool tileset. Gameplay reminds me quite a bit of 92-4.

6-4: The up-facing thwump thing was the best part of this, I think. It might work better having the two highest bounce blocks a little closer to the center so that you can jump from one to the other.

7-0: Gameplay is solid here. The turrets are well placed and balanced.

7-1: Excellent. The tile placement is spot on, perfectly suited to the laser. The exit switch is much harder than any of the other switches, but finally getting it is rewarding. I think the only really practical way is to use the rightmost tile on the leftmost structure.

7-2: Cool map with an interesting use of tile squeezes. The upper floorguard is brutal though.

7-3: Good and flowy in almost every section. I liked the fact that you used that oneway; it shows your attention to detail.

7-4: Getting to both exits is unique. Aesthetically, the map as a whole isn't very easy on the eyes.

8-0: I'm afraid I can't figure this one out. Whenever I lure the rocket out and get inside that little room I'm always killed by the mine above the exit switch or another rocket on the way down.

8-1: It's a decent puzzler. Nothing special.

8-2: I like the playparkish style. However, the gold delay thing might be a little too glitchy for Legacy. We'll see what the others have to say.

8-3: I wish it were easier to get the topmost gold first thing without the chainguns getting a clear shot. This felt average overall.

8-4: Very hard. I don't really like this style, which explains why I don't care for this map. Has a good flow to it though.

#138039 12 2006-02-01T01:46:36Z tktktk
I'm only commenting on ones that are new and some that are noticeably changed. And some that aren't new but I don't remember having played.

'Cross: Love this one, and it looks even better now.

Anthesic: Metanet city. The drone part is brilliant, the rest is good too, although the the bounce blocks are sadly unnecessary.

Bubble Bubble Splash!: Very likeable level with some good tense moments.

Club Baby Seals: Decent, not great. Nice flow.

Coiled: Great fast-paced drone hallway map.

Don't Blame The Stripes: I like it. It's different. Good work.

Facelift: If I'm not mistaken, this is half of one of your old levels. It's cool this way, and it's also fun using a shortcut to get to the exit switch.

Familiar: The drone timing is perfect. Love it. However, you can exploit the oneway glitch if a drone going up catches you in the gold column.

Flatline: Those drones are more effective than they have a right to be. Getting back up from the exit switch is a real pain.

Forth: Very easy, with a great flow if you do it right.

I May Have Killed It: Amazing. This plays so much better than the other version. Aesthetic point, though: you may want to move the exit half a snap to the right.

Last Minute: This looked really generic, but it turned out to be a very flowy and reasonably fun map.

Not Underneath: It's funny, I never see that width of angled tile hallways. Well, I guess it's not exactly funny, but you know what I mean. Or not. Whatever.

On Edge: Lovely. The gold is fun to get, and the gauss has you on the run when you're climbing to the top of the map. Great work.

Rappel: The gauss is very effective, and the mine/gold setup works well with it.

Rotational Mimicry: I love how you can angle jump between the two drones at the beginning. The tileset gives a surprising amount of maneuverability.

Scales: Whew. That rocket's always on your case, but it doesn't get too frustrating.

Sine Die: Keeps things interesting with multiple routes. I might have played this before, I'm not sure.

Space Heater: Nothing really special, but the multiple exits offer slightly different challenges.

Tauric: I think I failed to mention this earlier, but the thwumps don't work in case you didn't notice. I don't care for this one much at all.

Throes: Yes, this does indeed work better with lasers.

Unecessary, But Required: It's spelled "unnecessary", with two Ns. An all right map, I guess.

UPC: Is there another way of getting to the exit aside from corner jumping on the tile with the mine on it? That's the way I found.

Wobbly Bits: This does work better with the gold around the mines.

3D N would be fun, but id definitely wouldn't have the same... style.
I think the game can have completely the same experience, if one just solves the problem w/cameras

And kirby, I already saw that thread, but didnt Meta say the guy cant make the game "N" or he will be sued?
Getting the same experience with a 3D version of N would be virtually impossible. The main problem is that regardless of the camera angle, the entire map could never be seen at one time. It's often necessary to simultaneously track the location of enemies that are in two or three opposing directions, which can't very well be done in 3D space. The only feasible solutions would be multiple cameras or some kind of radar detection, but in all likelihood those would still be too confusing and unintuitive.

And yes, I believe work on that project has been discontinued.

#146888 8 2006-02-22T02:52:20Z tktktk
Great job so far, here are my comments on the new ones (and the few that may need changing, in bold):


0-0: I feel really silly getting so excited about something so simple, but this is really great. Very cool and stylized.

1-1: See previous comment.

2-3: Feels like a more systematic approach to a classic LV map. I like how the chute on the right side comes into play.

3-0: That seems like a very odd spot for the ninja to be placed... is it supposed to be there?

3-2: Drones look better when they're on top of gold (and mines) rather than under it.

3-4: The concept behind the side walls is very unique. An interesting little challenge.

4-0: Generic but cool race map. The inner ring of gold is surprisingly difficult to nab.

4-1: The concept is great, but it feels a little empty. As I said previously, it could do with some gold between the mines.

5-0: Very interesting level. The checkerboard layout gives it a distinctly strategic feel.

5-1: I like the gold arcs on top. The bottom is a bit more generic but still fun.

5-2: Absolutely brilliant. My only complaint with this is that you can simply hold left and right for guaranteed completion.

5-3: Very nice. I like how the rooms serve as safe havens from the drones.

5-4: Simple but great. Falling on the three little platforms after getting the exit switch feels incredibly intuitive.

6-2: Nice and easy with a good flow. The two tile width corridors make avoiding the gausses simple.

6-3: Very action oriented. Didn't find it particularly interesting, but there was certainly nothing wrong with it.

7-1: Hah. I was wondering what the point of this level was until I opened the doors and promptly collided with a newly rerouted drone.

7-2: Great design, very fun. Very maximo style, I think.

7-3: My initial reaction when seeing this level was dread and uncertainty. Luckily the tileset provides plenty of spots to evade the chainguns.

8-2: Weird map. Not much to criticize though, and I found getting the three switches strangely satisfying.

8-4: Another weird one. I liked the circle hopping at the end the best.

9-1: Fantastic small map if ever I saw one. Surprisingly difficult, and offers a real challenge if you're going for speed.

#152793 2 2006-03-08T07:17:36Z tktktk
Acoustic: Love the simple puzzleness. It might be cool if:
1) the mine below and to the left of the ninja (and the corresponding one) were taken out to give two paths to the bottom corner gold, or
2) some gold were added in the corridor below the ninja (and the corresponding one), which would take a little extra planning to get.

Ask Ze French: I friggin' love it. It's simple, fun, and flows perfectly.

Broken Escalators of Mayhem: Nice. The rocket/thwump combo gives a relatively unique element of strategy.

Continent: Oh yes. Another great one. However, the laser can be difficult to get past when rounding that upper left corner with the gausses always pressuring you.

Delegation Comes to Mind: Really hard. Cool, but really hard.

Disruptementalism: Oh yeah, I remember this one. Good stuff, to be sure.

Dronn: Like a Metanet level with the intensity and the number turned up several notches. Works, and works well.

I Never Did Trust Bubbles: Supremely flowy race-ish map, simple fun. Nice work.

I Think I Bit My Lip: Not your best, but interesting at least. Can't think of much to criticize.

If Gauss Could Kill: I enjoyed the fast pacing of this map immensely. Gliding up and down each column was somewhat difficult, but rewarding.

Makeshift Wings: I wanted to like this more than I did. The top felt kinda awkward to me, and the top corner gold looked a bit out of place.

Marginally Irrational: I find it very difficult to come up with pixelated-style maps like this that work effectively. This achieves its desired effect very well, however.

Saber or Justice: Creative. I liked the strategic routes you can use for speed demos and (presumably) all-gold runs.

Something to do with the Weight of the World: Not your best, not bad. It was kind of cool how if you took the side gold smoothly from top to bottom you'd end up jumping off of the thwump that was coming back up.

The I in Team is Lonely: Argh. I couldn't find a single reliable (as in few random deaths) method for beating this. The best way I could find was to drop down and walljump up one of the side walls, and that doesn't strike me as very good gameplay.

Some Kinda Monolith: Love the gold design, as well as the bizarre interface with the oneway and mine wall. Quirky and fun.

#152998 4 2006-03-09T01:33:17Z tktktk
About Contintent. In this and several of your Legacy maps you based the timing of everything on how long it takes to get the gold. The problem with this is that it doesn't allow as much for different play styles, and makes getting the gold semi-mandatory (you could just wait around, but no one wants to do that). It's not a huge deal, just a little thing I wanted to point out.

For I in Team, you're right, that method generally works very well. For the record, though, I'm not totally against any chaingun map that doesn't have stuff to hide behind. I also enjoy maps like this one. With open space chaingun maps, for me it's important that you can get quickly to another part of the map as the chaingun fires, or be able to control how the it fires by how you move as it charges up. I in Team is somewhere in between, and it doesn't totally work as an open space map or as a "bunker" map. However, your way of doing it works well enough that I don't think it necessarily needs to be changed or switched out.

#153911 7 2006-03-12T01:19:18Z tktktk
Quote: Kablizzy, March 11, 2006 04:00 am
Also, these are going to be our 80- and 90- columns that were missing from our initial launch, so the difficulties should be more diff...iculter...
While that definitely makes sense logically, I don't know if the public will go for that. There were several complaints of difficulty about the first 400 levels. Making both of these columns even harder than the 70s would not only make things hard to playtest, but also spark a lot of complaints from frustrated members. I just really doubt people will be as happy with this batch, no matter how good they are, if the majority can't beat them.

My suggestion is to make one column a "prequel" and one a "sequel", meaning one really easy column and one really hard one. The advantage of this is a balance of difficulty overall, and having something available for both experienced and inexperienced players. Although, in order to keep the levels in order of difficulty we'd have to name the levels in the prequel column "Negative 3-2" and whatnot.

So, kind of a radical idea, but just putting it out there.

#154303 14 2006-03-13T08:15:24Z tktktk
I think exact timing like "1.25 seconds" would be too hard to keep track of. Here's the best explanation I can give:

1. Hold right (or left) so that you're on horizontal ground and against a vertical wall.

2. Hold right (or left) for the duration of this tutorial.

3. Press the jump button twice as quickly as possible, and hold it the second time.

4. Briefly release the jump button just before you come into contact with the wall.

5. Immediately press and hold the jump button again right as you come into contact with the wall.

6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 as needed. Remember, if you time step 4 or 5 incorrectly it will result in a significant decrease in momentum.

Kablizzy Posted: March 04, 2005 10:54 am
Quote
Turn Ons:
Symmetry. I'm a symmetry freak. Make it symmetrical, and chances are, I'll love it.
Tradition. I like maps that stay within the accepted boundaries of map-making. The exception to this, of course, is unique ideas that are executed well. Boss Maps? No. Bug-only maps? Christ, no. Beyond that, I'm pretty lenient, so long as it's done well.
Simplicity. I can't stress how vital this is. I would rather have a map with one homing rocket than ten.

Turn Offs:
DDA maps where N dies, uses an excess of jump pads, or an excess of gold delay.
Asymmetrical maps. Not so much, but when a switch isn't centered, and it feels like it should be, it gets on my nerves. ESPECIALLY when it happens to one of my maps, grumble...
Levels where the mapmaker thinks it a superkewl idea to make one map with gausses, replace the gausses with homing rockets, replace the homing rockets with laser drones, so on and so forth until they have 5 of the same exact map with different enemies.
Maps where you have to delete the outside tiles. Come on, just no. The exception is James' DDA where N was vaulted 170 miles straight up, that was pretty cool. If the DDA hadn't lasted 11 minutes, it would have been downright awesome.
Maps that use hidden gausses, laser drones, et cetera. The one exception to this is hidden thwumps, but not by much.
Maps that aren't playtested properly. This is just a simple requirement. What kind of audacity do you have not to test if something works or not? A door bug here and there when you don't know about it, but I like playing through my levels prior to submitting, and I think I've only done this once or twice.
Unneccesary Map spam. I can see two, maybe three maps at a time, but once you get into a page, or two, or three, then you've got too many damn maps at once, and you need to take it outside. Because having that many maps in one day means that you've either been in a diabetic coma or your maps are crap.
Boss maps. I'd have to say this is the least of my pet peeves, but I still don't see the point, since the vast majority are awful.

Here are mine, nothing real special:

+ Symmetry. Not just for symmetry's sake, but in a way that both looks good and helps the gameplay.
+ Color variety. Blue from drones, red from mines, and yellow from gold make a level look visually pleasing.
+ Stylized. The kind of map that you can look at and play without knowing the author and say, "Oh yeah, so and so made this one."

- Rockets. Yes, this is sort of a contradiction, but there are sooo many rocket maps out there, and if yours doesn't do anything new with 'em it's just another map among hundreds of others.

- Unnecessary items. My biggest pet peeve, if there's a single mine or one-way that doesn't need to be there and isn't for aesthetic purposes, I hate it with a passion.
- Frustrating areas. I know, nobody likes them, but for me they can ruin the entire map in some cases.

Beo Posted: March 15, 2006 02:03 pm
Quote
Good:

- Good Gold Placement, I hate sloppily placed gold and overuse when the gold isn't properly placed. If you're going to use Z-snap, be extremely careful.
- Mines, maps just feel empty without at least a few.
- Planning, what I mean is that you can't make a tileset, slap some enemies on and call it a map. Have drone pathing that makes jumps that little bit trickier, a carefully placed floorguard to complicate an otherwise easy map. A nicely placed mine may force to take a completely different route
- Flow, maps have to have some kind of flow, even if they're action. This word also covers another design aspect, the pacing of the map. Make sure that it's not fast-paced and actiony one second, then slow and careful the next. If your map revolves around quickly changing playing styles, make sure you switch between the two at a steady pace, not at inconsistent intervals. Try to make your map flow between different gameplay styles.
- A variety of objects, it annoys me when maps have gold, mines and rockets [sometimes gausses.] If you're going to do that, make sure it's perfectly streamlined and you can't improve it. It's much better when more gameplay elements are woven together, to avoid mundanity
- Creativity, Freshness, come on, it's no fun playing the same map you've played hundreds of times before under a new disguise. try and innovate, or at least keep it fresh and blend styles together. Puzzle maps are great.
- Intelligence, I don't like playing maps mindlessly. Please make me at least think about which path to choose, how to execute a tricky jump, etc. Don't add hard enemies and think it's fun. Maps where you can choose your own path out of many, where there are several good ones but lots of bad ones so there's still strategy, that is, the freeform maps, are great fun.
- Aesthetics, please keep it neat, clean and stylish. There are endless tileset possibilities, don't stick with the one tile type and overuse pattern and shapes. Keep the style consistent, don't just abruptly change styles. You can make the map flow from one style from to another, just do it carefully and seamlessly

Bad:

- Bad Planning, maps where enemies are just slapped on and not thought about, with no attention to pathing and strategy
- Cluttering, where objects are bunched together and the maps looks ugly because of it.
- Linearity, make there be different paths, unless it's a puzzle where the whole fun is figuring out the one possible path to take.
- Be careful with chainguns, their main function is to force you to take refuge behind something or to keep moving as there is no real way to dodge them. In maps where the tileset and objects are designed to take advantage of this, then they're fine but avoid carelessly placing them anywhere.
- Plainess, use different kinds of tiles, enemies and gameplay and vary your maps because no one likes maps with one type of thing overused. Try to make it exciting and colourful. Never find a cool shape and copy it loads of times. It's just boring and ugly.
- Difficulty Spikes, as someone so aptly put it. When the map suddenly gets harder, or when the difficult bit is at the end and the player has to redo the easy parts over again to get to the part they're having difficulty with. 'There and Back' maps are annoying long, try to avoid any levels being excessively lengthy.

Looks pretty good overall. Edited for punctuation, wording, etc:

Quote: maximo, March 26, 2006 06:28 am
Theme: Episodes

This go around we are asking for a 5-map episode. The maps are to be episodic in nature and all that jazz. I'll explain the scoring shortly.

The rules are simple and are as follows:

-No bugs. If Metanet doesn't use it, you don't.
-All episodes must be submitted in .txt format attached to a post here or linked to a hosting service that has it (ihud is good place to host if you need a place to host a file).
-No editing of maps once they are judged. This is gonna go on an honor system, so please, if you are caught, you will suffer an undisclosed penalty, and trust me, you won't like it.
-All authors are allowed 1 submission, period. This is because we have to judge five maps per submission. So take your time and don't rush in your submission, because you can't submit then resubmit and just replace your old submission.
-Once you submit it is your final submission. You may edit a map until it is confirmed as submitted (as in I'll post and say you can't edit anymore because I'm going to put all these into one file for the judges).
-I haven't decided yet what the deadline for submissions will be, we'll see how it goes, but you will have at least a 1-week warning before it's over.
-Seeing as all scoring is based on judges' discretion, there will be a zero tolerance for any arguing of scores. If you would like to discuss a score, carry it out via PMs with the judge in question (aka, don't complain to me about someone else's review).
-It is your responsibility to check all scoring for your maps, not ours (and please check our math).
-If I forgot something, it's common sense. Don't be underhanded, and it should be fine.

And now for scoring:

Aesthetics (0-5): Do the maps look nice? I know this seems arbitrary to some, but it is important that you have some concept of form in your maps.
Rhythm (0-5): Do your maps have a flow to them? Do they work well for getting the gold? Are routes available that play well and fit the map and enemies? This will be one of the harder categories to get all 5 points on.
Difficulty (0-5): Are your maps ascending in difficulty, does the gold provided fit well with how the maps play in time for an episode. Are the maps "NUMA hard" or are they "episode hard" (which is easier)? If you want a benchmark for difficulty, shoot for the mid-late 70s column or less.
Length (0-5): Is this episode gonna take me 5 hours, because if so that could be a problem. The maps need to keep in mind that there are 5 of them and not just one (I'm a map counselor on the weekends).
Consistency (0-5): Do your maps suck halfway through, or do they shine throughout? Making sure each map is as good as the others is very important here. And just so you know, this means consistently good. Don't think putting up straight garbage will bag you 5 points here.
Judge's Opinion (0-25): This is where you make your money. You need to impress the judges, and really just make your maps stick in their minds, because we're gonna play a lot of maps and this is where you win or lose. Your maps need to convince us we are playing episodes made for the real deal. I want to forget I'm not playing the real game while playing your maps. Wow us and you'll get a bucket of points hot and fresh.

Judges:
Maximo
[working on it]

Backup judge:
Clovic

#159149 2 2006-03-29T02:30:27Z tktktk
OK, here's the transcript of PMs that started this Hall of Fame dealie. I took out the stuff that discussed who would be on the panel since it no longer applies. It's kinda lengthy, but everyone should at least skim through it to get an idea of what this thing is about.

Quote: tktktk
I want to get your opinion on something. In a few months I'm thinking about making some kind of "Greatest Maps of All Time" awards type thing. My main concern about this is that it would be too similar to the annual Dronies. However, the major difference is that any playable map from any place or date would be eligible for nomination, even the in-game levels. Voting would be much the same as the PM system for the Dronies, as that seemed to work very well. I would go with the point ranking system as well, but give people five slots to vote rather than three. Since there's only one thing to vote for, there would undoubtedly be more people voting, which translates to more extensive and accurate results.

Another idea is for this to become a sort of semi-Dronies that is done annually in the middle of the year. I believe that the Dronies name would be very beneficial to its popularity. Besides, there's bound to be a long drought in activity for the main Dronies, and this is the perfect thing to fill the gap. It's fine if you don't want this; I'm just throwing it out there.
Quote: sweep
I came up with an idea before The Dronies, which turned into the Dronies. It was basically an N Hall of fame. I'm thinking this could be pretty similar, if not a variant of that idea. I'd be up for this, but I think it needs a bit more thought... if you are suggesting it will happen mid-way through the year then web have plenty of time to think through general logistics.

It's a great idea, and infact, I think it should be a hall of fame, with new maps inducted every year. Maybe winners of past Dronies could automatically be part of the hall of fame, as well as a few "base" maps (eg Mount Doom). Then there could be a set amount of maps to be inducted each year, a specialist panel coming up with the initial list and then people voting on the list and as a result the set amount being inducted.

What do you think of this format as a possibility?

Sweep
Quote: tktktk
Sounds good, I think a Hall of Fame is something we're in need of. I don't know about the set amount of maps thing, though, as there might be more great ones in some years than others. Drony winners being inducted automatically makes sense. I assume the "base" maps would be selected by the specialist panel as well. The initial list would definitely need nominations from other people along with the panel's though, since otherwise some maps would almost inevitably be missed. However, the panel would reserve the right to edit the list as they see fit provided they inform everyone.

Heh, this seems like it will actually end up being bigger than the Dronies themselves. If we're lucky we might even be able to get Arachnid to make a Hall of Fame section of Numa.
Quote: sweep
I think they're two different things really. I mean, Hollywood Hall of Fames exist with Hollywood Awards shows, so why can't these two co-exist? The Dronies is more specialist, Hall of Fame more general... and they'll work together.
Quote: tktktk
Definitely, I agree. But will this thing still have the Drony name on it? I don't know if it needs to, but it should at least go along with it, be in the same subforum and all that.

My original goal with this was to find the map(s) that the community as a whole considers the best. For that reason I'd like for the base maps thing to be kept a secret until the public-chosen additions are revealed. We would have the base maps picked out in advance, and then later add a set number of public-chosen maps that aren't part of the base group. Does that make sense?

I suppose we'll have nominations end around May 31st, voting during June and the Hall of Fame additions revealed July 1st. That means (if we follow the Dronies model) that the whole shmear would be announced mid-April. These dates can all change, I'm just trying to figure out the basic time frame.
Quote: sweep
It could be called the N Hall of Fame, and just fit into the Dronies website and forum and everything, resulting in people considering it as basically the same thing (well, not the same... you know what I mean)
Quote: tktktk
Okay, yeah. That works. Do those dates sound about right to you?
Quote: sweep, 2006-03-28T07:48:43Z
Yeah, the dates seem fine.
Quote: tktktk
Right then. We still have to settle who's going to be on the panel, but besides that, anything else we need to discuss for the time being?
Quote: sweep
Nope.

I suggest that us two decide on the panel. I mean, as long as we don't miss someone I think it'll work out for the best that way.
Quote: tktktk
Something else just occurred to me. If this is supposed to be general and the Dronies are supposed to be specialized, it makes sense to switch out the category of Overall Map of the Year for Action Map of the Year. The Hall of Fame voting basically determines Overall Map of the Year anyway, right?
Quote: sweep
I'm not sure about the category thing. I mean, this is a hall of fame. Multiple winners. I'd suggest we don't reveal which maps got in with the most votes, I suggest we just say the ones that have made it in. This will allow the Dronies and the Hall of Fame to co-exist.
Quote: tktktk
I don't think saying how many votes each map got necessarily undermines the idea of multiple winners. People are curious to see which maps people enjoy more than others, and I'm pretty sure that showing the full results is a win-win for everyone.
